title: Constant right foot pain in a 62-year-old smoker
desc: This station involves a focused history and peripheral vascular examination of a 62-year-old woman in a rural ED with 3 weeks of constant right forefoot pain, then interpreting her observations, a bedside ankle-brachial index, bloods and a clinical photograph of the foot, and outlining escalation, transfer, analgesia and safety netting.
focus: Recognising chronic limb-threatening ischaemia from the history and examination, and escalating it from a rural ED
stem: You are a senior medical student in the Emergency Department of a busy rural hospital. Petunia, a 62-year-old woman, has come in after a visit from the community nurse today, when she said she has had constant pain in her right leg. Your consultant has asked you to review her. A nurse is with you, has taken her observations and can carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Petunia and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, a bedside ankle-brachial index, her blood results and a clinical photograph of her foot. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Petunia, a 62-year-old retired station cook. You are not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. You are sitting on the edge of the trolley with your right leg hanging over the side and a sock still on your right foot. You are uncomfortable but chatty, a bit dismissive of the problem, and you play down your smoking and drinking until pressed. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (if the candidate asks, or at once if they do not): "Her obs are all within the flags: BP 162/88, heart rate 86 and regular, sats 96% on room air, temperature 36.8. She won't lie flat on the trolley and keeps hanging her leg over the side. She hasn't wanted anyone to take the sock off yet."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask you to lie flat (for example to examine you), the pain gets worse within a minute: "Oh, that's worse, I need to hang it down." It eases when you hang the leg down again.
  • If the candidate explains why they need to look at your foot and asks to remove the sock, you agree reluctantly and wince as it comes off. Do not refuse.
  • If they offer pain relief, the nurse gives it and the pain eases to about 3/10 over the next 15 minutes.
  • If they explain things kindly and without jargon, you relax and answer more openly about smoking and alcohol.

Opening line: "I had a nurse come around today that said I needed to get checked out for my walking..."

History (give only when asked):

The pain

  • Site: the front of your right foot and the toes. It does not spread anywhere else.
  • Quality: burning.
  • Severity: 5/10.
  • Onset and course: it came on 3 weeks ago and has been constant since.
  • Worse: at night in bed, or lying on the couch.
  • Better: hanging your feet off the side of the bed. You have been sleeping half sitting up with the leg over the edge.
  • Impact: you have not been able to leave the house for 3 weeks.
  • The foot itself: you have not looked at it, because it hurts too much to take the sock off. You do not know whether there are any sores or colour changes.

Before this (only if asked about previous episodes or walking)

  • You used to get pain in your legs when walking. You are not sure of the distance, but you would have to stop about 10 to 15 times while doing the shopping. Resting for a minute or two made it go away.
  • That pain was different from this one: it only came on with walking and went with rest. This pain is there all the time.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all negative)

  • No swelling, warmth or redness of the calf or leg. No calf pain.
  • No back pain, no numbness or weakness in the legs, and the walking pain was not eased by leaning forward on the shopping trolley or sitting.
  • No fevers or sweats, no discharge, smell or wetness from the foot that you know of.
  • No painful red lumps along the veins, no fingers going white or blue in the cold, no joint pains, no tiredness or weight loss, no change in vision, no fainting.
  • No chest pain or palpitations lately. No new weakness or speech problems.
  • The pain did not start suddenly; it built up over a day or two.

Past medical history

  • High blood pressure, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes. The community nurse comes monthly to check your sugars and blood pressure.
  • A heart attack 5 years ago and a stroke 2 years ago. You made a good recovery from the stroke.
  • The stroke was a clot (ischaemic). You were given aspirin after the heart attack but stopped it yourself a few years ago because you "didn't see the point". No stomach bleeds or ulcers.
  • No arthritis, lupus or other autoimmune disease, no vasculitis, no clotting or bleeding problems, no cancer.

Medications

  • Rosuvastatin 20 mg in the morning.
  • Ramipril/felodipine CR 2.5 mg/2.5 mg in the morning.
  • Metformin 500 mg at night.
  • Nothing else: no aspirin or other blood thinner now (you stopped the aspirin yourself, as above), no over-the-counter medicines.

Allergies: none known.

Family history

  • Both parents had type 2 diabetes.
  • Your mother died of a heart attack at 53. Your father died of a stroke at 60.

Social history

  • You live with your husband on a station 50 km out of the closest town.
  • Retired; you used to cook for the workers on the station.
  • Alcohol: "a couple of stubbies with dinner". If asked about weekends: about 8 stubbies a night on Friday and Saturday.
  • Smoking: at first say, "I smoked a bit when I was younger, but not too much." If asked for detail: 20 a day from age 15 to 50, and 10 a day since you were 50. You have never tried to quit.
  • Never used recreational drugs.
  • Diet: meat and chips most nights, not many vegetables.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it is "just bad circulation" from getting older and that it will settle down. You are worried about being away from home, because your husband relies on you and town is a long drive. You expect some tablets for the pain and to go home today. If the candidate seems worried, ask: "It's not serious, is it?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: overweight woman sitting with the right leg dependent, uncomfortable, alert. Nicotine staining of the right index and middle fingers. Observations as the nurse reported.
  • Pulse and BP: radial pulse 86/min, regular. BP right arm 162/88, left arm 158/86.
  • Heart and neck: dual heart sounds, no murmurs. No carotid bruits.
  • Abdomen: soft, no pulsatile or expansile mass.
  • Shins (visible on inspection): both hairless with thin, shiny skin.
  • Feet (only if the sock is removed and the feet inspected): right foot: the big toe, second and third toes are black, dry and shrivelled, and the blackening extends onto the medial forefoot over the first metatarsal head, with a sharp line of demarcation from the surrounding skin. The fourth toe is dusky blue. The rest of the foot is pale and shiny with no hair. No discharge, no surrounding redness or swelling, no smell, no heel ulcer. Thickened toenails. Left foot: no ulcers, no gangrene, nothing between the toes.
  • Colour with position: the right foot is dusky red while hanging down.
  • Temperature: right foot cold to the mid-foot; left foot cool.
  • Capillary refill: right fourth and fifth toes more than 5 seconds; left toes 3 seconds.
  • Pulses: femoral pulses palpable on both sides, the right weaker, with a right femoral bruit. Popliteal: right absent, left palpable. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial: right both absent; left dorsalis pedis weak, left posterior tibial palpable.
  • Buerger's test: on elevation the right foot goes white at about 15 degrees; when hung over the side it slowly turns deep red over about 30 seconds. The left foot goes pale at about 50 degrees.
  • Calves: soft, non-tender, equal in size, not warm, no swelling or redness.
  • Neurology: reduced monofilament sensation over both forefeet; vibration reduced at the left big toe and at the right medial malleolus (the right big toe cannot be tested). Power 5/5 throughout. Ankle reflexes reduced on both sides.
  • Spine: not tender, full flexion, straight leg raise negative on both sides.
  • Ankle-brachial index: if the candidate says they would measure it, say the result will be given in Part 2.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a senior medical student, confirms Petunia's identity and explains the consultant asked them to review her.
Acknowledges her pain, offers analgesia early and lets her keep the leg hanging down for comfort. Asks about smoking and alcohol without judgement, in plain language.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site: right forefoot and toes, no radiation
Burning, 5/10, came on 3 weeks ago and has been constant since
Worse lying in bed or on the couch, eased by hanging the foot over the side of the bed
Impact: has not left the house for 3 weeks

check.x: Asks about earlier walking pain: pain on walking that went with rest, stopping 10 to 15 times while shopping, and establishes that it was different from the current constant pain.
Asks about tissue loss: sores, ulcers, colour change or blackening of the toes, and whether she has looked at the foot (she has not).
Asks about features of the differentials:

kids.x: Lumbar spinal stenosis: back pain, leg numbness or weakness, relief by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping trolley
Vasculitis: migratory thrombophlebitis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, joint pain, visual change, syncope
Infection of the foot: fever, discharge, smell, spreading redness
Other history: autoimmune disease, clotting disorders and cancer (none)

check.x: Takes the cardiovascular past history: hypertension, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction 5 years ago and stroke 2 years ago.

Takes the medication history (rosuvastatin 20 mg, ramipril/felodipine 2.5/2.5 mg, metformin 500 mg) and allergies (none), notes she is on no antiplatelet despite a previous MI and stroke, and asks why (stopped herself; no bleeding history; stroke was ischaemic).
Takes a family history: both parents with type 2 diabetes, mother died of an MI at 53 (premature), father died of a stroke at 60.
Quantifies smoking beyond "a bit": 20 a day from 15 to 50 and 10 a day since, about 40 pack-years, current smoker who has never tried to quit.
Quantifies alcohol including the weekend pattern (2 stubbies a night, 8 a night at weekends), and asks about diet and recreational drugs.
Asks about home and function: lives with her husband on a station 50 km from town, retired cook, housebound for 3 weeks.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is bad circulation that will settle, worried about leaving her husband, expects tablets and to go home.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs, including the pulse rhythm (regular, so an embolic source such as AF is less likely) and BP in both arms.

Removes the sock and inspects both feet, including between the toes and the heels. Identifies dry gangrene of the right great, second and third toes and medial forefoot with a dusky fourth toe, trophic changes, and no signs of infection.
Compares temperature and capillary refill of both feet (right cold to the mid-foot, CRT more than 5 seconds).
Palpates the pulses on both sides:

kids.x: Femoral pulses, listening for a bruit (right weaker with a bruit), and palpates the abdomen for an aortic aneurysm
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses (both absent on the right)

check.x: Performs Buerger's test and interprets it: pallor at about 15 degrees and slow dependent rubor show severe ischaemia on the right.
Examines the calves and foot sensation (monofilament or vibration); spine/SLR not required.
States they would measure an ankle-brachial index with a handheld Doppler.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all in the white zone, afebrile, elevated BP (grade 2 range, likely partly from pain; on treatment), pain worse lying flat. States that normal observations do not lessen the limb threat, and that escalation is driven by the foot, not the chart.
Interprets the ABI: right 0.28 with ankle pressures below 50 mmHg and monophasic signals means severe ischaemia that fits chronic limb-threatening ischaemia; left 0.78 means PAD in the other leg too.

Notes that calcified vessels in diabetes can falsely raise the ABI, so a low result is reliable. Interprets the bloods: normal WCC and CK with a minimally raised CRP (no sign of infection or acute muscle death); HbA1c 9.1% (poor control); LDL 3.4 mmol/L, well above target; eGFR 58, which matters for contrast imaging.
Describes the photograph: dry gangrene of the first three toes and medial forefoot with clear demarcation, a dusky fourth toe that is threatened, and no wet gangrene, pus or cellulitis.

Gives the diagnosis as chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg with tissue loss (dry gangrene) from atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease. Justifies it with rest pain for more than 2 weeks, eased by dependency, gangrene, the ABI and her risk factors.

Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against, including acute-on-chronic limb ischaemia/atheroembolism and painful diabetic neuropathy (others accepted: claudication alone, lumbar spinal stenosis, DVT, Buerger disease).
Management
Escalates at once to the consultant and phones the on-call vascular registrar at the nearest tertiary hospital, sending the ABI and the photograph.

Arranges urgent transfer to the tertiary vascular centre through the retrieval or patient flow service for arterial imaging and assessment for revascularisation or amputation. Does not discharge her home.
Gives analgesia: regular paracetamol with titrated opioid, and lets the leg hang dependent. Avoids elevating the leg.
Protects the foot: keeps the gangrene dry with a dry non-adherent dressing, offloads the heels, no compression stockings and no debridement in the ED.

Secondary prevention agreed with vascular, after confirming the stroke was ischaemic and there is no bleeding history: single antiplatelet, intensified statin, BP/glucose control and smoking cessation with NRT offered.
IV access, ECG for AF and BGL monitoring; asks vascular about fasting.
check.d: Also accept (not required): withholds metformin while fasting, and after contrast if AKI, eGFR below 30 or first-pass intra-arterial contrast.

check.x: Explains in plain words that the blood supply to the foot is badly blocked and part of it has died. Answers honestly that she may lose part of the foot, explains why transfer cannot wait, involves her husband and checks understanding and consent.
Safety netting

While she waits for transfer, asks the nurse for regular foot observations (colour, warmth, sensation, movement, pain) and tells Petunia and the nurse to report at once: sudden worse pain, the foot becoming colder, numb or weak, spreading dark colour, the foot turning wet, red, swollen or smelly, fever, chest pain or stroke symptoms.
Names any two follow-up services she will need after discharge: vascular follow-up, high-risk foot service, GP review of secondary prevention.

part2.lead: Here are her observations, the bedside ankle-brachial index, her blood results and a clinical photograph of her right foot taken in the department.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4; do not interrupt the management answer.

  • "Can't I just go home tonight and come back next week? Who'll look after my husband and the station?"
  • "Are they going to cut my foot off?"

You are frightened by the possibility of losing part of your foot and go quiet. If the candidate explains honestly and kindly why you need to go to the bigger hospital now, you agree, and ask whether your husband can be called. If they give vague reassurance or use jargon, say: "So it's not that bad then?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. She lay flat for the Doppler measurements from about 14:00 to 14:05; the 14:15 set was taken after she sat up with the right leg hanging over the side of the trolley.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, BP 162/88 rising to 168/90, HR 86 rising to 94 and regular, temperature 36.8 to 36.9 °C, alert: every value is in the white zone. BP 162 to 168/88 to 90 is in the white zone but in the grade 2 hypertension range (systolic 160 to 179), likely partly from pain, despite ramipril and felodipine. Pain rose from 5 to 6 out of 10 after lying flat.
  • Meaning: no sepsis and no physiological instability. The small rise in HR, BP and pain came from lying flat, which is typical of ischaemic rest pain. The regular rhythm makes an embolic source less likely.
  • Changes: the chart calls for no clinical review or rapid response. Review BP control as part of secondary prevention once the pain is controlled. The urgency comes from the threatened limb, so she still needs escalation to vascular surgery, analgesia, leg dependency and regular foot observations.

rows.note: Triage: sitting with right leg dependent
Pain worse lying flat for Doppler despite analgesia at 13:20; now sitting with leg over side

handover.label: Bedside ankle-brachial index
handover.result:
Bedside ankle-brachial index, handheld continuous-wave Doppler (8 MHz), measured by the ED registrar at 14:05 after 5 minutes supine, which she tolerated with difficulty because of pain.

SiteRightLeft
Brachial systolic pressure162 mmHg158 mmHg
Dorsalis pedis systolic pressure40 mmHg, monophasic118 mmHg, biphasic
Posterior tibial systolic pressure46 mmHg, monophasic126 mmHg, biphasic
Ankle-brachial index (higher ankle pressure / higher brachial pressure)46/162 = 0.28126/162 = 0.78

Other Doppler signals: right common femoral biphasic but damped; right popliteal monophasic and damped. Toe pressures not measured (no equipment on site).

Reference: ABI 1.00 to 1.40 normal; 0.91 to 0.99 borderline; 0.90 or below abnormal; above 1.40 non-compressible vessels.
handover.model:
• Read: right ABI 0.28 with both ankle pressures below 50 mmHg and monophasic pedal and popliteal signals; left ABI 0.78 with biphasic signals. Brachial pressures are equal, so there is no subclavian disease to distort the result.
  • Meaning: severe ischaemia on the right. An ABI below 0.4 and an ankle pressure below 50 mmHg support CLTI alongside her rest pain and gangrene. The damped popliteal signal with a weak femoral pulse and bruit suggests multilevel disease (iliofemoral and femoropopliteal). Left ABI 0.78 is PAD in the other leg too. In diabetes, calcified arteries can falsely raise the ABI, so a low value like this is reliable, though the true severity may be worse.
  • Changes: this confirms a limb-threatening problem needing urgent vascular review and imaging; send the numbers with the referral.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 13:40 after medical review. No previous results on this hospital's system.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb, WCC, neutrophils and platelets normal. CRP 12 is only slightly raised. CK and lactate are normal. Creatinine 94 with eGFR 58 is mild renal impairment and there is no baseline. Random glucose 11.2 and HbA1c 9.1% show poorly controlled diabetes. LDL 3.4, HDL 0.9 and triglycerides 2.6 are an atherogenic profile despite rosuvastatin 20 mg. INR and APTT are normal.
  • Meaning: no laboratory sign of infection (dry, not wet, gangrene) and no acute muscle necrosis. Her uncontrolled risk factors are driving the disease.
  • Changes: antibiotics are not needed now. The eGFR is passed on because she will need iodinated contrast for CT angiography. The eGFR is passed on for contrast planning. At eGFR 58 with no AKI, metformin can continue for CT angiography (IV contrast); withhold it on the day she is fasting for a procedure, and from the time of contrast for 48 hours if she has AKI, eGFR below 30 or intra-arterial contrast with first-pass renal exposure, then recheck eGFR before restarting (RANZCR; local protocol). Monitor BGL. (Accepted, not required.) Normal clotting and a group and hold already done prepare for a procedure. Secondary prevention needs intensifying: lipid lowering toward LDL below 1.8 mmol/L (below 1.4 mmol/L per ESC 2024 accepted) and better glucose control.

rows.n: target with established vascular disease (<1.4 per ESC 2024)

handover.label: Clinical photograph of the right foot
handover.result:
Clinical photograph of the right foot, dorsal and medial views, taken in the ED at 13:50 for the vascular referral.

  • Great, second and third toes: black, dry, shrivelled and hard, with no blistering or discharge.
  • Medial forefoot: black, dry skin extending over the first metatarsal head, with a sharp line of demarcation from the surrounding skin.
  • Fourth toe: dusky blue discolouration.
  • Rest of the foot: pale, shiny and hairless; thickened toenail on the fifth toe.
  • Surrounding tissue: no redness, swelling, pus or moist tissue. No ulcer on the heel or between the toes.
handover.model:
• Read: dry gangrene of the first three toes and the medial forefoot with a clear line of demarcation; the dusky fourth toe is critically ischaemic and at risk; trophic changes over the rest of the foot; no wet gangrene, cellulitis or pus.
  • Meaning: established tissue loss from severe ischaemia. With 3 weeks of rest pain this is CLTI, and the forefoot involvement puts the limb at high risk. It is dry, so it is not an infective emergency today, but it can turn wet.
  • Changes: send the photograph with the vascular referral. Keep the foot dry and protected, give no antibiotics unless infection appears, and watch for the foot becoming wet, red or smelly, which would need urgent antibiotics and surgical review.

ask: You are now calling the on-call vascular registrar at the tertiary hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Petunia, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Petunia now, here in this rural emergency department.

Petunia asks you whether she can go home to the station tonight. Please answer her, then tell me what you would ask the nurse to watch for while she waits for transfer, and name two services she will need for follow-up after discharge.
expect:
• Identify: self, senior medical student in the rural ED; Petunia, 62.
  • Situation: 3 weeks of constant right forefoot rest pain with dry gangrene of the first three toes and medial forefoot; threatened fourth toe.
  • Background: previous claudication; hypertension, dyslipidaemia, T2DM, MI 5 years ago, ischaemic stroke 2 years ago; about 40 pack-years, current smoker; no antiplatelet (stopped aspirin herself, no bleeding history).
  • Assessment: obs all white zone, afebrile, regular rhythm; no right popliteal or pedal pulses; right ABI 0.28, ankle pressures below 50 mmHg; left 0.78; WCC and CK normal, CRP 12, so no infection; HbA1c 9.1%, LDL 3.4, eGFR 58. Right CLTI with tissue loss.
  • Recommendation: please accept for urgent transfer and imaging; advice on antiplatelet, anticoagulation and fasting.

Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, right leg, with dry gangrene from atherosclerotic PAD: 3 weeks of rest pain, worse lying flat, eased by dependency; previous claudication; gangrene; absent right popliteal and pedal pulses; positive Buerger's test; ABI 0.28; heavy smoking, diabetes, MI, stroke.

Core differentials:

  • Acute-on-chronic ischaemia or atheroembolism: for: onset over 1–2 days, dusky fourth toe; against: power 5/5, no new numbness, regular rhythm.
  • Painful diabetic neuropathy: for: diabetes, burning night pain, reduced sensation and reflexes; against: eased by dependency, absent pulses, ABI 0.28, gangrene.

Also accepted (third differential): claudication alone (now constant with tissue loss); lumbar spinal stenosis (not eased by flexion, normal spine); DVT (soft, non-tender calves); Buerger disease (age 62, atherosclerotic risk factors).

1. Escalate and transfer: consultant, then phone the tertiary vascular registrar with the ABI and photograph; urgent transfer through the retrieval or patient flow service; not home.
  2. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly plus titrated opioid (for example oxycodone immediate-release 2.5 to 5 mg orally); leg dependent, not elevated.
  3. Foot care: keep dry, dry non-adherent dressing, offload heels, no compression, no debridement.
  4. Work-up: IV access, ECG for AF, BGL monitoring; ask vascular about fasting; group and hold already done; eGFR 58 for contrast. Accepted: At eGFR 58 with no AKI, metformin can continue for CT angiography (IV contrast); withhold it on the day she is fasting for a procedure, and from the time of contrast for 48 hours if she has AKI, eGFR below 30 or intra-arterial contrast with first-pass renal exposure, then recheck eGFR before restarting (RANZCR; local protocol). Monitor BGL.
  5. Secondary prevention agreed with vascular, after confirming the stroke was ischaemic and there is no bleeding history: aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily; intensify statin; BP and glucose control; smoking cessation with NRT offered.

• Answer: no. The blood supply to the foot is badly blocked and part of it has died; without urgent specialist treatment she could lose more of the foot or the leg. Honest that some of the foot may need to be removed, and that the team will try to improve blood flow. Offers to call her husband; checks understanding and gains her agreement to transfer.
  • Nurse to watch for and call at once: regular foot checks (colour, warmth, feeling, movement, pain); sudden worse pain, colder, numb or weak foot, spreading dark colour, foot turning wet, red, swollen or smelly, fever, chest pain or stroke symptoms.
  • Follow-up (any two): vascular follow-up, high-risk foot service, GP review of secondary prevention.

ddx.dx: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg with dry gangrene, from atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease
ddx.for: Three weeks of constant burning forefoot pain that is worse lying flat and eased by hanging the leg, after years of claudication, with gangrene of three toes, absent right popliteal and pedal pulses, right ABI 0.28 and heavy cardiovascular risk.

ddx.dx: Intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease
ddx.for: She used to stop 10 to 15 times while shopping with walking pain that went with rest.
ddx.against: The current pain is constant at rest and there is tissue loss, so she has moved beyond claudication.

ddx.for: She has type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 9.1%, burning pain worse at night, reduced monofilament and vibration sense and reduced ankle reflexes.
ddx.against: The pain eases when she hangs the leg down, and absent pulses, an ABI of 0.28 and gangrene show the pain is ischaemic.

ddx.dx: Acute-on-chronic limb ischaemia (thrombosis on existing disease) or atheroembolism
ddx.for: The pain built up over a day or two 3 weeks ago and the fourth toe is dusky.
ddx.against: She has no new numbness or weakness, power is 5/5 and her rhythm is regular, with a stable 3-week course.

ddx.for: She had leg pain on walking that eased with rest.
ddx.against: The pain was not eased by leaning forward or sitting, she has no back pain, her spine examination is normal, and her foot pulses are absent with an ABI of 0.28.

ddx.for: She has unilateral leg pain, has been housebound for 3 weeks and smokes.
ddx.against: Her calves are soft, non-tender and equal with no warmth or swelling, and the pain is in the toes and eased by dependency.

guide:
In Part 1, Petunia answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Describe the gangrene only if the candidate removes the sock and inspects the foot. Toe capillary refill, colour with position, foot temperature and pedal pulses can only be given once the sock is off. If they do not remove it, give no foot findings and do not mark item 18; the photograph in Part 2 still lets them interpret it. If they ask for the ABI or bloods in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order, reading out Petunia's question for the last one. Petunia then asks her questions in Part 2 as scripted.

A high-performing candidate recognises rest pain from the positional pattern (worse lying, better hanging down), separates it from her earlier claudication, quantifies the smoking despite her playing it down, and notices she is on no antiplatelet after an MI and a stroke and asks why. They take the sock off, find the gangrene, and work through pulses, Buerger's test and the differentials. In Part 2 they read the ABI correctly and recognise that normal observations do not lessen the threat to the limb. They name CLTI with tissue loss, escalate to the tertiary vascular registrar and arrange transfer, give analgesia with the leg dependent, protect the foot, and answer Petunia honestly.

A borderline candidate takes a reasonable pain history but calls it claudication or neuropathy, never looks at the foot, accepts "a bit" of smoking, and plans outpatient review or a GP referral. Sending her home is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

Petunia has chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) of the right leg with tissue loss. The Global Vascular Guidelines define CLTI as peripheral arterial disease with ischaemic rest pain, gangrene, or a lower limb ulcer present for more than 2 weeks. Objective tests support it: an ankle pressure below 50 mmHg, an ABI below 0.4, a toe pressure below 30 mmHg or a low transcutaneous oxygen. She has rest pain for 3 weeks, dry gangrene of three toes and the medial forefoot, and a right ABI of 0.28 with ankle pressures below 50 mmHg. The guidelines stage the limb with WIfI (Wound, Ischaemia, foot Infection). Her foot has extensive tissue loss reaching the forefoot (W3), severe ischaemia (I3: ABI below 0.4, ankle pressure below 50 mmHg) and no infection (fI0), clinical stage 4, which puts it at high risk of amputation without revascularisation.

The history that makes the diagnosis

  • Rest pain: constant burning in the forefoot and toes (the most distal tissue), worse lying flat or at night because gravity no longer helps perfusion, and eased by hanging the foot over the bed. Patients often sleep sitting up with the leg dependent.
  • Progression from claudication: her earlier walking pain, stopping 10 to 15 times while shopping and relieved by rest, was vascular claudication.
  • Risk factors: age; hypertension, dyslipidaemia and type 2 diabetes; previous MI and stroke (disease in other arterial beds); about 40 pack-years of current smoking; alcohol above NHMRC guidance, especially at weekends; a poor diet; and premature cardiovascular death in her mother.
  • A missed opportunity: she is on no antiplatelet despite established coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Ask why: she was given aspirin after her MI and stopped it herself. Before restarting an antiplatelet, confirm the stroke was ischaemic (not a bleed) and that there is no history of bleeding or peptic ulcer; both are confirmed here.

Vascular versus neurogenic claudication

Claudication is pain deep in the leg muscles (calf, thigh or buttock) on activity, relieved by rest. Vascular claudication comes on after a set distance. Ask about everyday scenarios: can they walk around the shopping centre without stopping, how many stops, can they walk to the letterbox? It is worse walking uphill. Neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis is brought on by walking downhill or by standing (for example chopping vegetables). It is relieved by sitting and leaning forward or leaning on a shopping trolley, and walking uphill is easier.

Examination

Take the sock off and inspect both feet, including between the toes and the heels. A patient who has not looked at her own foot may have tissue loss nobody knows about. Look for trophic changes (hairless, shiny skin, thick nails), compare temperature and capillary refill, and feel the femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses on both sides. Listen for a femoral bruit and feel for an aortic aneurysm. Buerger's test shows pallor on elevation (an angle below about 20 degrees means severe ischaemia) and slow dependent rubor. Check the calves, foot sensation (diabetic neuropathy is common and matters for foot protection) and the spine. An irregular pulse would raise the possibility of an embolic cause.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations are all in the white zone. A threatened limb does not show on a general observation chart, so escalation rests on the clinical findings.
  • ABI: 0.90 or below is abnormal, and below 0.4 is severe. Her right ABI of 0.28 with monophasic signals fits CLTI, and her left ABI of 0.78 shows disease in the other leg. Calcified arteries in diabetes and kidney disease can make the ABI falsely normal or high, so toe pressures are used when the ABI is not reliable. A low ABI, as here, is reliable.
  • Bloods: a normal WCC, a near-normal CRP and a normal CK argue against infection and acute muscle death. The HbA1c and lipids show uncontrolled risk factors. The eGFR matters for iodinated contrast.
  • Photograph: dry gangrene with clear demarcation and no infection, and a threatened fourth toe.

Differentials

Intermittent claudication alone does not explain constant pain with tissue loss. Painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy also causes burning foot pain worse at night, and she does have neuropathy (reduced monofilament, vibration and ankle reflexes), but neuropathic pain is not relieved by hanging the leg down and does not explain absent pulses, an ABI of 0.28 or gangrene; the two often coexist, and neuropathy can blunt ischaemic symptoms. Acute limb ischaemia (sudden pain, pallor, coldness, loss of sensation or movement, often from AF), and acute-on-chronic ischaemia from thrombosis on existing disease or atheroembolism to a toe, is a separate emergency. Her onset over a day or two and the dusky fourth toe keep it in mind, but her stable 3-week course, normal power and regular rhythm argue against it; new numbness or weakness would change the urgency to hours. Lumbar spinal stenosis causes leg pain, weakness and numbness that ease with lumbar flexion, with normal pulses. DVT causes calf swelling, warmth, redness and a dull ache. Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) affects young heavy smokers and is diagnosed only after excluding other causes; it causes distal ischaemia, migratory thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon.

Management in a rural ED

  1. Escalate immediately to your supervisor and the vascular registrar on call at the nearest tertiary hospital, with the ABI and a clinical photograph.
  2. Analgesia: regular paracetamol with titrated opioid. Let the leg hang dependent and do not elevate it.
  3. Transfer to the tertiary centre through the retrieval or patient flow service. There she will have arterial imaging (duplex, CT angiography or angiography) and be assessed for endovascular or open revascularisation, and for amputation of the non-viable tissue.
  4. Work-up before transfer: IV access, ECG for AF, BGL monitoring and fasting as the vascular team advise (group and hold is already done). At eGFR 58 with no AKI, metformin can continue for CT angiography (IV contrast); withhold it on the day she is fasting for a procedure, and from the time of contrast for 48 hours if she has AKI, eGFR below 30 or intra-arterial contrast with first-pass renal exposure, then recheck eGFR before restarting (RANZCR; local protocol). Monitor BGL.
  5. Foot protection: keep dry gangrene dry and covered, offload the heels, no compression and no ED debridement. Antibiotics only if infection or wet gangrene develops.
  6. Secondary prevention (eTG): once the stroke is confirmed ischaemic and there is no bleeding history, a single antiplatelet (aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily); statin therapy intensified toward LDL below 1.8 mmol/L (below 1.4 mmol/L with at least a 50% reduction per ESC 2024), for example rosuvastatin 40 mg and/or adding ezetimibe 10 mg; and control of BP and diabetes. Agree the timing with the vascular team, who may change antithrombotic therapy around a procedure; the vascular team may consider rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin. Smoking cessation is the most important modifiable step: brief advice, nicotine replacement in hospital (patch plus a short-acting form) and a Quitline referral.

Safety netting and follow-up

While she waits, the nurse does regular foot observations and calls at once for sudden worse pain, a colder, numb or weak foot, spreading discolouration, a foot that becomes wet, red, swollen or smelly, fever, or chest pain or stroke symptoms. After the tertiary admission she needs vascular follow-up, a high-risk foot service or podiatry, GP review of her secondary prevention and diabetes, smoking cessation support and community nursing. She lives 50 km from town, so she should call 000 for sudden foot or chest symptoms rather than drive in.
points: Ischaemic rest pain is constant forefoot and toe pain, worse lying flat or at night and eased by hanging the leg down. Present for more than 2 weeks, or with gangrene or an ulcer, it defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
Always take the sock off and inspect both feet, including between the toes and the heels. A patient in pain may never have looked at her own foot.

ABI 0.90 or below is abnormal and below 0.4 is severe; an ankle pressure below 50 mmHg supports CLTI. Calcified vessels in diabetes can falsely raise the ABI, so use toe pressures when it looks normal.

Normal observations do not make a threatened limb safe. In a rural ED, escalate CLTI the same day to the tertiary vascular registrar and arrange transfer, with analgesia, leg dependency and a dry, protected foot.
Vascular claudication comes on after a set distance and is worse uphill. Neurogenic claudication is worse downhill or standing and is relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping trolley.
CLTI is a marker of widespread arterial disease. Start an antiplatelet, intensify lipid lowering, control BP and diabetes, and treat smoking cessation as part of the treatment.
